input: This passage presents a capital appraisal for a warehouse extension, the purpose of which is to establish whether the expected savings from the project are sufficient to justify its installed cost. The installed cost of the extension is $1575k, and the expected net saving is $271k per year, which is expected to continue for 8 years. Discounting these savings at a discount rate of 8% gives a present value of the savings of $1557k, and when the installed cost is set against this figure, the net present value of the project works out at $-18k. It is important to appreciate that the savings figures used in this appraisal are vendor and utility estimates, and that no saving has yet been measured on a comparable installation, so the outcome of the appraisal rests on estimates that have not so far been confirmed in practice. The appraisal accordingly brings together the three elements that any such comparison requires: a capital figure that is incurred at the outset, a stream of savings that is expected to accrue evenly over the life of the project, and a rate at which those future savings are discounted in order to express them in present terms, and it is only when all three elements have been combined that the project can be said to have been appraised at all.
target:
The warehouse extension has a net present value of $-18k at a discount rate of 8%. The present value of the expected savings ($1557k) falls short of the installed cost ($1575k), so on the stated figures the savings do not repay the investment within the appraisal.

The appraisal rests on an expected net saving of $271k per year for 8 years. Discounted at that rate, those savings give the present value above; undiscounted, the same savings would exceed the installed cost, and the shortfall arises from discounting alone. The decision therefore turns on the discount rate and on the savings estimate, not on the arithmetic.

The appraisal is a comparison of two money figures at one point in time: what the extension costs to install, and what the savings are worth when each year's saving is reduced to its present value at the stated rate. A saving received later is worth less than the same saving received sooner, and discounting is the operation that expresses that difference; discounting, rather than the size of the savings, carries the result below zero. The finding is therefore marginal in size but not in sign.

The savings are vendor and utility estimates. No saving has yet been measured on a comparable installation, so the negative result carries the uncertainty of the estimates themselves: a measured saving below the estimate would deepen the shortfall, and the appraisal gives no measured figure against which the estimate can be checked.
